title: Explaining Rankings with Hidden Group Bonuses

paper.title: Explaining Rankings with Hidden Group Bonuses
paper.abstract: Abstract. Determining a linear utility function that correlates with observed candidate rankings is a foundational problem with applications in domains such as admissions, hiring, and recommendation systems, e.g., [Storandt and Funke, AAAI’19, Zhang et al., KDD’23, Wang et al., ICDE’24 (best paper award), Chen and Wong, VLDB’24]. Traditionally, these models assume full visibility into the feature sets used to determine the utility score. However, real-world scenarios often involve sensitive attributes that are hidden or partially observed, yet may influence outcomes through additive bonuses designed to promote fairness, as in [Gale and Marian, ICDE’24]. Motivated by such practical concerns, we study a variant of the ranking explanation problem where sensitive features are unobserved but may influence candidate rankings through group-specific linear boosts. We present a formal framework for modeling this problem and develop an algorithmic solution that leverages constraint satisfaction and automated reasoning techniques to jointly infer the linear scoring parameters and latent group bonuses consistent with the observed rankings. We further show that determining a satisfying linear function with group-specific bonuses is NP -hard in general, but when the feature dimension and the number of groups are constant, the problem admits a polynomial-time solution. Our approach is the first to address this nuanced variant, which captures key real-world challenges in fair ranking and admission systems. We perform extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets, demonstrating that our method effectively recovers hidden bonus structures and provides faithful explanations of observed ranking outcomes.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Ranking algorithms are central to numerous AI applications, including web search, recommender systems, and information retrieval. However, despite their pervasive use, the decision-making processes behind these algorithms often remain opaque, which raises critical concerns around trust, fairness, and accountability. As a result, explainability in ranking has emerged as a pressing research challenge within the AI community. Several recent works have sought to adapt principles from interpretable machine learning to the ranking setting ( Chowdhury et al., 2023 ; Chowdhury et al., 2025 ; Heuss et al., 2025 ) , aiming to generate faithful, user-understandable explanations for ranked outputs. Some approaches focus on post-hoc explanations, while others design models that are easier to interpret from the start ( Singh and Joachims, 2019 ; Ai et al., 2018 ) . There is also increasing attention to broader goals like fairness and trust in ranked results ( Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017 ; Rampisela et al., 2024 ) . Yet, many basic questions remain open: what does it mean for a ranking to be explainable? How do we measure the quality of an explanation when the output is an ordered list instead of a single label? Modeling user preferences is a central challenge in multi-criteria decision-making. A common and effective approach is to formalize these preferences with a utility function that assigns a numerical score/utility to each candidate, thereby inducing a natural ordering. Candidates are typically characterized by a set of features, which can be distinguished as scoring attributes – that directly contribute to utility, and sensitive attributes – used to enforce auxiliary goals such as fairness or diversity. Among various functional forms, linear utility models are arguably the most widely adopted. Their prevalence stems from a powerful combination of simplicity and practical efficacy. The straightforward structure of a weighted sum not only facilitates deployment in large-scale systems like web search and recommender engines ( Morik et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2023 ; Thonet et al., 2022 ) but also offers inherent transparency ( Sen et al., 2020 ; Gale and Marian, 2020 ) . This transparency, simplicity, and effectiveness make linear utility-based models a natural starting point for research into explainability and learning to rank ( Asudeh et al., 2019b ; Chen and Wong, 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , interactive learning ( Nanongkai et al., 2012 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , reverse regret ( Wang et al., 2024 ) (best paper award at ICDE’24), and the integration of fairness and diversity mechanisms ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Despite their simplicity, linear utilities have demonstrated competitive performance, confirming their status as a robust and versatile modeling choice, e.g., ( Qian et al., 2015 ; Storandt and Funke, 2019 ) . We refer the readers to Section 7 for a more elaborate discussion on related works. Several works have studied how to quantify the distance between a given ranking and one induced by a (linear) utility function. Common notions include the number of violated pairwise orders, the distance to a consistent utility vector, and the minimum perturbation needed to make the ranking “linearizable”. Exact computation is often intractable in the presence of conflicting preferences, motivating the study of approximation and structural relaxations (e.g., ( Dwork et al., 2001 ; Davenport and Kalagnanam, 2004 ) ). In many real-life scenarios, a small additive bonus is essential to ensure that a linear utility-based ranking model aligns with observed outcomes. Such a bonus is primarily calculated based on the sensitive attributes ( Shetiya et al., 2022 ; Asudeh et al., 2019a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) – separate from the scoring attributes used to compute utility – associated with each candidate or item. This often arises when external goals, such as affirmative action, fairness constraints, or prior trust scores, must be incorporated uniformly across items of certain groups. The application of compensatory additive bonuses to linear utilities is an approach that has been explored for promoting fairness in ranking systems ( Gale and Marian, 2024 ) . Without such a term, even simple adjustments to promote underrepresented groups may not be achievable within the linear feature space, making the additive bonus a minimal yet powerful mechanism for enforcing policy-driven interventions (see ( Mathioudakis et al., 2020 ) ). Consider a public university conducting its annual admissions, where applicants are ranked using a linear utility-based model . Academic performance is assessed through multiple indicators, such as entrance test and SAT scores, which are normalized, weighted, and linearly aggregated to compute a base utility score. As a public institution committed to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), the university augments this model with an additive incentive mechanism . Recognizing that applicants from underprivileged (UP) backgrounds may face structural disadvantages affecting academic performance, an expert committee assigns a group-specific bonus score. sections.heading: Problem (Informal) Formulation
sections.text: Given a ranking, can it be explained by a linear utility function with a small number of additive bonuses? In the Singleton Group Bonus Linear Ranking ( SGBLR ) version, arbitrary bonuses may be given to at most k k items. In the g g -Group Bonus Linear Ranking ( g g -GBLR ) version, there are g g (special) groups each containing a limited number of items, and group-specific bonuses – each item of a particular group gets the same amount as a bonus, and bonus value for different groups could be different – are allowed. The goal is to find weights and bonus assignments that reproduce the ranking exactly. Note that Example 1 is for the 1 1 -GBLR variant with one (special) group being UP – all the candidates of the UP group receive an additive bonus of the same amount. Our method conceptually builds upon seminal works LIME ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ) and SHAP ( Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ) , which infer feature contributions to predictions, as our model learns weights for each feature, which provides an explanation for the observed ranking. It extends this line of work by modeling hidden additive bonuses beyond observable features as part of the explanation. We envision our technique as contributing to the broader area of trustworthy and responsible data science, particularly in applications such as algorithmic auditing and explainability. For example, in an auditing setting, suppose a ranking model is used to evaluate candidates, and there is a requirement that all candidates within the same group receive identical bonuses. If our method is unable to recover a linear utility function with such additive bonuses that explains the observed ranking, this serves as evidence that the ranking violates the intended fairness constraint. Alternatively, our framework can be used for interpretability. If an observed ranking can be well-approximated by our model, the learned weights provide insight into the relative importance of different attributes, while the inferred additive bonuses reveal how much advantage may have been assigned to specific candidates. This can help assess whether such adjustments are reasonable within the given domain and context.

sections.heading: 1.1. Our Contributions
sections.text: In this paper, we initiate a formal study on the problem of learning a linear utility function with small additive group-wise bonuses that realizes a given ranking. On the theoretical side, we provide exact algorithms and establish computational hardness. Next, we address the question of designing scalable algorithms that work efficiently in practice. More specifically, we show the following results. • We start by considering the singleton group variant ( SGBLR ) that captures the allowance of arbitrary (potentially different) additive bonuses to a few individual items. We design a hyperplane-based algorithm – enumerating over all the regions specified by a set of comparison hyperplanes, and then performing certain longest common subsequence (LCS) computation in each region. Our algorithm works in polynomial time for constant-dimensional points. We further extend our algorithm to a more general variant of group-wise bonuses ( g g -GBLR ) by introducing a new auxiliary dimension per group, leading to an algorithm that runs in polynomial time for a constant number of groups and for constant-dimensional points. Note that often in practice, both the number of groups and the dimension of the feature vectors are indeed small (bounded by some constant). • We complement our algorithmic results with computational hardness. The problem, even if in its simplest form of singleton groups, is NP -hard for arbitrary dimensions, establishing that the exponential dependency on dimension of our algorithm is unavoidable assuming P ≠ \neq NP . • While the theoretical algorithm establishes tractability in principle at least for constant dimension, its high complexity motivates us to explore more practical alternatives using modern ILP solvers. We formulate the problem as an MILP and evaluate its performance using state-of-the-art solvers. • We conduct extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets to demonstrate the efficacy and scalability of our methods. In case of SGBLR we observe that for two-dimensional data the MILP formulations scale well, whereas the computational hardness inherent in the hyperplane-based algorithm prevents it from scaling beyond small instances. In the case of g g -GBLR with g = 1 g=1 , the MILP formulations exhibit strong scalability with respect to both dimensionality (up to d = 17 d=17 ) and the number of tuples (up to approximately 75,000 75{,}000 ). For the real-world dataset, containing around 300,000 300{,}000 tuples, the MILP formulations successfully handle the g g -GBLR problem for both g = 1 g=1 and g = 2 g=2 , highlighting their practical applicability at large scale.

sections.heading: Problem formulation
sections.text: For our first problem setting, we consider finding a bonus-aware linear function that realizes a given ranking π \pi where the number of tuples that receive a bonus is at most k k . Definition 1 ( SGBLR ). Given a set of tuples 𝒟 = { t 1 , t 2 , … ​ t n } \mathcal{D}=\{t_{1},t_{2},...t_{n}\} where each t i ∈ ℝ d t_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , a target ranking π \pi over the tuples and an integer k k , does there exist a linear utility function s w s_{w} with w ∈ ℝ d w\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a bonus vector v ∈ ℝ n \textbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with at most k k non-zero values such that sorting the tuples by s w ​ ( t i ) + v i s_{w}(t_{i})+v_{i} produces the ranking π \pi ? In practice, an estimate of the number of tuples belonging to under-represented groups is often available. The SGBLR problem captures the lower bound on the number of tuples that need to be allotted a bonus for a linear function to realize π \pi . The number of under-represented groups is typically a small known number (usually constant), and thus it would be of interest to find a bonus-based linear utility function that respects the number of groups g g . We now propose the g g -GBLR problem. Definition 2 ( g g -GBLR ). Given a set of tuples 𝒟 = { t 1 , t 2 , … ​ t n } \mathcal{D}=\{t_{1},t_{2},...t_{n}\} where each t i ∈ ℝ d t_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , a ranking π \pi over 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and integer k k . sections.heading: Algorithm for SGBLR
sections.text: We first present our approach, and then provide an argument about its correctness. Consider the d d -dimensional weight-space. For every pair of tuples t i t_{i} , t j t_{j} introduce the comparison hyperplane 𝒞 i , j \mathcal{C}_{i,j} in this space. We term the set of these ( n 2 ) \binom{n}{2} hyperplanes as ℋ \mathcal{H} . Introduction of ℋ \mathcal{H} to the ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} dimensional weight-space partitions it into numerous regions, which is termed the arrangement of hyperplanes ( Edelsbrunner, 1987 ) . As each weight-function in this space lies either below or above the comparison hyperplanes , the ranking that is realized corresponds to a unique ranking. The set of all functions that have the same ranking in the arrangement can be shown to be a convex region and corresponds to a “ cell " of the arrangement. To formalize this, consider a vector of ( n 2 ) \binom{n}{2} boolean signs corresponding to each utility function termed as the location vector . A location vector is of the form { + , − } ( n 2 ) \{+,-\}^{\binom{n}{2}} . A similar argument follows for − - . sections.heading: Analysis of ERMB
sections.text: The analysis of our algorithm relies on two steps: (i) enumeration of the cells of the arrangement, and (ii) LIS of the sequences ρ \rho . To prove the complexity of the enumeration step, we rely on Corollary 28.1.2 of ( Toth et al., 2017 ) . The corollary states that the number of such regions with n n hyperplanes in d d -dimensional space is bounded by 𝒪 ⁡ ( n d ) \mathcal{O}(n^{d}) . We state the Corollary below for easy access. Proposition 3 . ( Toth et al., 2017 ) The maximum combinatorial complexity of an arrangement of n n hyperplanes in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} is 𝒪 ⁡ ( n d ) \mathcal{O}(n^{d}) . Moreover, if the arrangement is simple, its complexity is indeed Θ ⁡ ( n d ) \Theta(n^{d}) . Observe that each hyperplane C i , j C_{i,j} as shown in Equation 2 has an intercept of 0 0 and hence passes through the origin. Therefore, the resulting arrangement is a special case of a hyperplane arrangement known as a central arrangement (see ( Schneider, 2022 ) for details). In a central arrangement, the combinatorial complexity of a central arrangement with m m hyperplanes in d d dimensions is 𝒪 ⁡ ( m d − 1 ) \mathcal{O}(m^{d-1}) (see ( Schneider, 2022 ) Chapter 5). Thus, in our case, n 2 n^{2} hyperplanes in d d -dimensional weight space form a central arrangement, which bounds the number of unique rankings realizable to 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ ( d − 1 ) ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2(d-1)}) . This helps us in establishing 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ d + 1 ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2d+1}\log n) bound on the time complexity (see Appendix C ). Now, consider the region of the arrangement of 𝒞 i , j \mathcal{C}_{i,j} where the vector w ∗ w^{*} lies in. Let w w be the vector in this region that our algorithm picks, and let ρ \rho be the resulting ranking from ordering t ∈ 𝒟 t\in\mathcal{D} in decreasing order of their scores. For any pair of points t 1 , t 2 ∈ 𝒟 t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathcal{D} that receive no bonus from v ∗ v^{*} , it is clear that w ⋅ t 1 > w ⋅ t 2 w\cdot t_{1}>w\cdot t_{2} if and only if w ∗ ⋅ p 1 > w ∗ ⋅ t 2 w^{*}\cdot p_{1}>w^{*}\cdot t_{2} . Therefore, both ρ \rho and π \pi must have the same total order over points in 𝒟 \mathcal{D} that receive no bonus from v ∗ v^{*} . These points are a lower bound on the length of the LCS of π \pi and ρ \rho , so our approach must find a w w , v v which satisfies SGBLR with v v at least as sparse as v ∗ v^{*} . ∎ Improved Running Time for 2 2 -dimensions. We remark that in the special case of d = 2 d=2 , the enumeration step (line 4 of Algorithm 1 ) can be performed very efficiently as the weight space is now 1 1 -dimensional. Therefore, each comparison hyperplane is a point partitioning the line. Enumeration of the regions can thus be done in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2}\log n) time by sorting the comparison hyperplanes, followed by a linear scan to obtain the ranking and then performing a LIS on each ranking, leading to an overall running time of 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 3 ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n^{3}\log n) (compared to an worse bound of 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 5 ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n^{5}\log n) implied from Theorem 1 ). We use this faster implementation in our experiments.

sections.heading: 3.2. Algorithm for g g -GBLR
sections.text: The budgeted group setting is more intriguing as Algorithm 1 cannot directly be adapted to this setting, because the notion of a fixed number of groups is not modeled in SGBLR . In this section, we first embed the idea of bonus into the weight space and then design a polynomial-time algorithm for the fixed dimension, fixed group setting. We treat group bonuses as bonus dimensions , expanding the feature space to d + g d+g dimensions – one additional dimension per group. Then, to handle group membership, the algorithm generates g + 1 g+1 copies of each tuple: one base version and one for each group membership (whether it belongs to a particular group or not). It then uses hyperplane arrangements in this augmented space to enumerate all possible rankings of the expanded dataset. Unlike simpler cases that use Longest Increasing Subsequence, this approach requires us to employ a budgeted Longest Common Subsequence (LCS). A dynamic programming routine aligns the target ranking π \pi with these candidate rankings to find the optimal solution that strictly respects the group size constraints. We provide a detailed description of the algorithm and analysis in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4. Hardness Results
sections.text: In this section, we show that the problem of linear realizability of a ranking with additive group bonuses is NP -hard. Theorem 1. SGBLR is NP -hard. To show the above, we provide a reduction from a variant of the classical Max-2-SAT , namely Max-1-in-2-SAT . Definition 2 ( Max-1-in-2-SAT ). Given a 2-CNF formula, and a non-negative integer r r , the problem is to decide whether there exists an assignment of variables that satisfies at least r r clauses by making exactly one literal (out of two literals) in each of these r r clauses to be true. The above problem is known to be NP -hard by a straightforward reduction from MaxCut – another classical NP -hard problem. In fact, the problem remains NP -hard even for monotone formulas. Theorem 3 (Folklore). Max-1-in-2-SAT is NP -hard. Reduction from Max-1-in-2-SAT . Suppose we are given an instance of the Max-1-in-2-SAT problem: A 2-CNF formula F F over n n variables x 1 , ⋯ , x n x_{1},\cdots,x_{n} , with m m clauses C 1 , C 2 , ⋯ , C m C_{1},C_{2},\cdots,C_{m} (without loss of generality assume that m < n 2 m<n^{2} ), and a non-negative integer r r . Then we construct an instance of the decision version of the SGBLR problem as follows: For each clause C i C_{i} , create a point p i ∈ ℝ n p_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} by setting, p i ​ [ j ] = { 1 if ​ x j ​ appears in ​ C i − 1 if ​ x ¯ j ​ appears in ​ C i 0 otherwise . p_{i}[j]=\begin{cases}1\quad\quad\quad\text{if }x_{j}\text{ appears in }C_{i}\\ -1\quad\quad\;\text{if }\bar{x}_{j}\text{ appears in }C_{i}\\ 0\quad\quad\quad\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} Further, take ℓ = ( m + 1 ) ​ n 2 \ell=(m+1)n^{2} additional points: q 1 = ⋯ = q ℓ = 0 n q_{1}=\cdots=q_{\ell}=0^{n} . Consider the dataset 𝒟 := ∪ i = 1 m { p i } ⋃ ∪ i = 1 ℓ { q i } \mathcal{D}:=\cup_{i=1}^{m}\{p_{i}\}\bigcup\cup_{i=1}^{\ell}\{q_{i}\} . Then, consider the following ranking π := q 1 ⪯ ⋯ ⪯ q n 2 ⪯ p 1 ⪯ q n 2 + 1 ⪯ ⋯ ⪯ q 2 ​ n 2 ⪯ p 2 ⪯ ⋯ ⪯ q ℓ − 2 ​ n 2 + 1 ⪯ ⋯ ⪯ q ℓ − n 2 ⪯ p m ⪯ q ℓ − n 2 + 1 ⪯ ⋯ ⪯ q ℓ \pi:=q_{1}\preceq\cdots\preceq q_{n^{2}}\preceq p_{1}\preceq q_{n^{2}+1}\preceq\cdots\preceq q_{2n^{2}}\preceq p_{2}\preceq\cdots\preceq q_{\ell-2n^{2}+1}\preceq\cdots\preceq q_{\ell-n^{2}}\preceq p_{m}\preceq q_{\ell-n^{2}+1}\preceq\cdots\preceq q_{\ell} . The instance of the decision version of the SGBLR problem would constitute 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , ranking π \pi , and the non-negative integer m − r m-r . We defer the soundness and completeness proof to Appendix E . Remark 4 . It is worth noting that SGBLR is a special case of the more general g g -GBLR problem, where each group could be of arbitrary size. Thus NP -hardness of SGBLR immediately establishes a similar hardness for g g -GBLR . Furthermore, one may note that our reduction works even when there are only two (non-singleton) groups with bonuses.

sections.heading: 5. Scalable Frameworks via MILP
sections.text: The geometric algorithm introduced earlier provides an exact, constructive way of identifying valid rankings through hyperplane arrangements. However, such geometric reasoning scales poorly with the number of data points n n and dimensions d d , since the number of combinatorial regions grows exponentially. Even for moderate d d , enumerating or traversing these regions becomes practically intractable. To design a more scalable alternative, we reformulate g g -GBLR problem as a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) — a mature framework that allows us to express logical ordering and grouping constraints in a linear-algebraic form, solvable by powerful off-the-shelf engines. The MILP formulation represents ranking relationships through a set of linear inequalities defined over two classes of variables — continuous feature weights w w and binary membership indicators δ i ​ r \delta_{ir} . Each inequality enforces the required order between tuples in terms of their weighted feature scores and group bonuses. This formulation connects combinatorial ranking constraints with continuous optimization, allowing discrete ordering relations to be reasoned about using standard MILP solvers.

sections.heading: 5.1. 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} Formulation
sections.text: We first define the base formulation, denoted as 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} , which represents the canonical encoding of the ranking constraints: minimize 0 subject to ∑ j ∈ [ d ] ( t i ​ [ j ] − t ( i + 1 ) ​ [ j ] ) ⋅ w j + ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ i ​ r ⋅ v r − ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ ( i + 1 ) ​ r ⋅ v r ≥ 0 ∀ i < n ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ i ​ r ≤ 1 ∀ i ∈ [ n ] ∑ i ∈ [ n ] ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ i ​ r ≤ k δ i ​ r ∈ { 0 , 1 } , v r ≥ 0 ∀ i ∈ [ n ] , r ∈ [ g ] | w j | ≥ 1 ∀ j ∈ [ d ] \begin{array}[]{lll}\text{minimize}&0&\\ \text{subject to}&\sum_{j\in[d]}(t_{i}[j]-t_{(i+1)}[j])\cdot w_{j}+\sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{ir}\cdot v_{r}&\\ &-\sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{(i+1)r}\cdot v_{r}\geq 0&\forall i<n\\ &\sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{ir}\leq 1&\forall i\in[n]\\ &\sum_{i\in[n]}\sum_{r\in[g]}&\delta_{ir}\leq k\\ &\delta_{ir}\in\{0,1\},v_{r}\geq 0\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \forall i\in[n],&r\in[g]\\ &|w_{j}|\geq 1&\forall j\in[d]\end{array} Here, w ∈ ℝ d w\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the feature weights to be learned, v r v_{r} denotes the additive group bonus for group G r G_{r} . We introduce g ⋅ n g\cdot n binary indicator variables δ i ​ r \delta_{ir} for i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] and r ∈ [ g ] r\in[g] , where δ i ​ r \delta_{ir} is 1 if tuple t i t_{i} belongs to group G r G_{r} , otherwise 0 0 . The constraints encode ordering, group capacity, uniqueness, non-negativity, and weight-magnitude requirements. The objective is to minimize 0 (i.e., this is a feasibility problem), which means the ILP seeks any feasible solution satisfying all constraints that respects the ranking π \pi . Notice that the 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} formulation remains generic and domain-agnostic: it treats all features and groups symmetrically, without leveraging problem-specific insights. In many real-world settings, additional knowledge—such as bounds on group influence, or on pre-identified boosted tuples—can meaningfully restrict the feasible space and guide the solver toward more computationally efficient solutions. Incorporating such application-driven structure motivates a refined formulation, 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} , described next.

sections.heading: 5.2. 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} Formulation
sections.text: 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} – The refined formulation tightens the feasible region by incorporating domain/application-informed assumptions and introducing solver-oriented constraints that eliminate redundant solutions and enhance numerical stability. 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} introduces the following enhancements: (1) Strict ordering with tolerance: To ensure a clear and stable ranking, we introduce a small positive margin ϵ \epsilon between consecutive tuples. This enforces a strictly decreasing order of adjusted scores rather than allowing equality, thereby avoiding ties and improving numerical stability during optimization. We adopt a strategy similar to that of prior work ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . In our experiments, we set ϵ \epsilon as 10 − 5 10^{-5} , which ensured sufficient spacing between tuple scores, thus accommodating floating-point tolerances. (2) Bounded additive bonuses: Each group’s additive bonus is constrained within a predefined range to prevent it from dominating the linear utility function. These bounds capture realistic limitations on how much a group-specific adjustment can influence the overall ranking. We emphasize this bound is not a restriction of 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} , and can be changed based on expectations of the range using domain knowledge. (3) Non-negative feature weights: In many real-world settings, such as performance evaluation or credit scoring, features contribute positively to the final score. Accordingly, all feature weights are constrained to be non-negative, reflecting domain semantics and eliminating redundant sign symmetries in the optimization process. We emphasize that this assumption is not a limitation of 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} ; if a feature is known to contribute negatively to the final utility, one can appropriately scale the feature values to ensure this. (4) Dominated tuples: Under the assumption that feature weights are non-negative, we use the standard idea of dominance followed in monotone functions ( Börzsönyi et al., 2001 ) . If it is observed that there exists a pair of tuples where t j t_{j} dominates t i t_{i} , yet t i t_{i} is ranked before t j t_{j} , then it is guaranteed that t i t_{i} must have received an additive bonus. Therefore, we add the constraint that t i t_{i} must belong to one of the groups receiving a bonus by adding a constraint ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ i ​ r = 1 \sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{ir}=1 . Finding the set of points that dominate at least one other point yet are ranked lower can be formulated as a skyline query ( Börzsönyi et al., 2001 ) . To this end, the dataset is augmented with an additional dimension representing the rank of each tuple. Specifically, for a tuple t i t_{i} , we append its rank in π \pi as the ( d + 1 ) (d+1) th dimension. On the resulting augmented dataset, we compute the skyline—where larger values are preferred in every dimension—using the Double Divide-and-Conquer ( DDC ) algorithm, which runs in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ log d − 1 ​ n + n ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(n\log^{d-1}n+nd) time ( Kung et al., 1975 ) . Any tuple that is dominated by another must necessarily receive a bonus. This procedure can be repeated iteratively until no additional dominated tuples are identified. The complete 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} model is thus: minimize 0 subject to ∑ j ∈ [ d ] ( t i ​ [ j ] − t ( i + 1 ) ​ [ j ] ) ⋅ w j + ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ i ​ r ⋅ v r − ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ ( i + 1 ) ​ r ⋅ v r ≥ ϵ ∀ i < n ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ i ​ r ≤ 1 ∀ i ∈ [ n ] ∑ i ∈ [ n ] ∑ r ∈ [ g ] δ i ​ r ≤ k 0 ≤ v r ≤ 100 ∀ r ∈ [ g ] w j ≥ 0 ∀ j ∈ [ d ] \begin{array}[]{lll}\text{minimize}&0&\\ \text{subject to}&\sum_{j\in[d]}(t_{i}[j]-t_{(i+1)}[j])\cdot w_{j}+\sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{ir}\cdot v_{r}\\ &-\sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{(i+1)r}\cdot v_{r}\geq\epsilon&\forall i<n\\ &\sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{ir}\leq 1&\forall i\in[n]\\ &\sum_{i\in[n]}\sum_{r\in[g]}\delta_{ir}\leq k&\\ &0\leq v_{r}\leq 100&\forall r\in[g]\\ &w_{j}\geq 0&\forall j\in[d]\end{array}

sections.heading: Relationship Between 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} and 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}}
sections.text: The relationship between the two formulations is hierarchical. The feasible region of 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} is a strict subset of that of 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} , ensuring that every refined solution remains sound under the base model. While 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} defines a broad feasibility space, 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} incorporates additional structure—such as bounded bonuses and restricted membership subsets—that enhances interpretability, aligns with domain semantics, and yields more realistic solutions. In essence, 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} serves as the foundational declarative model, whereas 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} is its solver-optimized and practically scalable counterpart.

sections.heading: 6. Experimental Evaluation
sections.text: We now present an empirical evaluation of our proposed formulations and algorithms. The primary goals of this experimental evaluation are to assess scalability and practical applicability, and to compare the proposed methods with one another and with suitable baselines. We examined both real-world and synthetic datasets to understand how the models behave under diverse data distributions and parameter settings.

sections.heading: Experimental environment.
sections.text: All experiments were run on a server with an AMD EPYC 7763 CPU, with 128GB of RAM allocated for each experiment, running Ubuntu 24.04. All code is implemented using Python 3.12.3 with Gurobi version 12.0.2 as the MILP solver. Gurobi and implemented algorithms were allowed to use up to 16 threads. The timeout was considered 1800 seconds. Datasets. We evaluate our methods on one real-world dataset and a set of synthetically generated datasets. Real-world data. The real-world dataset, introduced in prior work ( Cai, 2025 ) , contains examination scores of 384,977 candidates who took the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE) in India in 2009. After removing entries with missing values, 384,970 candidates remain, each described by three numerical attributes—Mathematics, Physics, and Chemistry scores—and categorical attributes such as gender and reservation category. We use the three numerical scores as equally weighted features. Categorical attributes define groups receiving additive bonuses. In single-group experiments, female candidates receive a bonus of 4, reflecting the median score difference from male candidates. In two-group experiments, candidates from underprivileged categories receive a bonus of 6, and female candidates receive a further bonus of 4, corresponding to their median differences from the general (GE) category. These data-driven adjustments preserve the original score distribution while modeling group-level advantages.

sections.heading: Synthetic data
sections.text: We also construct multiple synthetic datasets to systematically evaluate scalability. Each dataset 𝒟 = { t 1 , t 2 , … , t n } \mathcal{D}=\{t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n}\} consists of n n tuples, where each tuple t i t_{i} is a d d dimensional feature vector. Each feature component t i ​ [ j ] t_{i}[j] is sampled independently from a uniform distribution over [ 0 , 25 ) [0,25) and rounded to two decimal places. A linear weight vector W = ( w 1 , … , w d ) W=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{d}) is sampled similarly. To introduce structured deviations from a purely linear ranking, additive bonuses are assigned to randomly generated groups of tuples. For each group G r G_{r} , a bonus v r v_{r} is sampled uniformly from [ 5 ​ d , 10 ​ d ) [5d,10d) . For 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} , a random subset 𝒟 ′ ⊆ 𝒟 \mathcal{D}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{D} is first selected, and groups are then formed by uniformly sampling tuples from 𝒟 ′ \mathcal{D}^{\prime} . Each tuple’s augmented score is computed as f ⁡ ( t i ) = ∑ j = 1 d w j ​ t i ​ [ j ] + v r f(t_{i})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}w_{j}t_{i}[j]+v_{r} if it belongs to G r G_{r} , and as f ⁡ ( t i ) = ∑ j = 1 d w j ​ t i ​ [ j ] f(t_{i})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}w_{j}t_{i}[j] otherwise. Finally, tuples are sorted in decreasing order of their augmented scores to yield the target ranking π \pi . This generation process models ranking scenarios in which a base linear utility function is modified by sparse, group-level adjustments, providing a controlled ground truth for evaluation.

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: We consider three baselines for comparison. We use ordinal regression ( Srinivasan, 1976 ) as the first baseline, where ranks are used as the ordinal predictor values. As a second baseline, we apply logistic regression by creating a dataset of all pairs of tuples. For a pair t i t_{i} ranked above t j t_{j} , the tuple t i − t j t_{i}-t_{j} is labeled 1 1 , and t j − t i t_{j}-t_{i} labeled 0 0 . This results in a supervised learning task with binary labels, on which standard logistic regression can be applied. Both of these baselines output a linear utility function, and given this function, the number of tuples that need to be given a bonus to realize the input function is computed. We also consider a simple baseline, called LocalSearch , which repeatedly samples a random unit vector as the weight function within the given time limit. For each sampled weight vector, it computes the minimum number of tuples that must receive an additive bonus to realize the target ranking π \pi . The best-performing weight vector – i.e., the one minimizing the number of required bonuses – is returned as the final output. Our experimental evaluation examines both the computational performance and the solution quality of the proposed formulations and algorithms.

sections.heading: Results: RQ2, RQ3 and RQ4 – One Group Setting
sections.text: Considering practical formulation of the MILP-based formulations, 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} and 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} , we now turn to RQ2–RQ4, where we study the scalability of these approaches under varying parameters. In particular, we analyze their behavior as we vary the dimensionality d d , the number of tuples n n , and the group size k k . Regarding RQ2 – As shown in Figures 2(a) and 2(b) , for fixed tuple sizes of n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 and n = 50,000 n=50{,}000 respectively (with k k set to 0.1 ​ n 0.1n ), the runtime of both 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} and 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} increases as the dimensionality d d grows. For n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 , the impact is particularly evident for 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} , which times out beyond d = 5 d=5 . In contrast, 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} remains tractable and scales up to d = 17 d=17 within 450 seconds. This demonstrates that incorporating domain-specific structure significantly improves the scalability of 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} . However, when increasing the dataset size to n = 50,000 n=50{,}000 , even 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} times out for dimensions above d = 11 d=11 . This indicates that while the refined formulation extends scalability, high-dimensional large instances remain computationally challenging at larger scales. An additional scalability challenge in higher dimensions is the degradation of the skyline pruning, which is part of 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} . Skyline pruning is extremely effective at d = 2 d=2 , with around 95% of the tuples that are boosted being identified by skyline pruning. When d = 5 d=5 , the effect diminishes significantly, with around 5% of the tuples identified, and at d ≥ 8 d\geq 8 the skyline pruning is unable to identify tuples that are definitely boosted. Regarding RQ3 – For two-dimensional data, the increase in tuple size has only a modest impact on runtime. Although we observe a slight increase in execution time as n n grows, both 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} and 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} exhibit comparable performance in this setting. The detailed figure is presented in Appendix A (Figure 7 ). However, for d = 8 d=8 , as shown in 2(c) , the situation changes markedly. Even at n = 2,000 n=2{,}000 , 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} already times out, clearly indicating that dimensionality has a far more significant effect on computational cost than the number of tuples. For d = 8 d=8 , 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} remains scalable up to 50,000 50{,}000 tuples; beyond that point, solver-level heuristic changes introduce noticeable performance variance. Regarding RQ4 – MILP solvers exhibit irregular and non-monotonic behavior: small changes in k k often lead to substantial fluctuations in runtime. This behavior is typical for MILPs. Although modifying k k only alters the tightness of the capacity constraints ∑ i δ i ​ r ≤ k \sum_{i}\delta_{ir}\leq k , such changes can significantly affect the strength of the MILP relaxation, the size of the feasible region for the δ \delta -variables, the degree of symmetry in the model, and ultimately the structure of the branch-and-bound tree explored by the solver. As a result, the runtime may increase or decrease unpredictably. This phenomenon is also observed in our experiments. For example, with n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 and d = 5 d=5 , 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} exhibits pronounced runtime peaks at intermediate values of k k (in the range of 10–50%), whereas 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} remains consistently faster while still reflecting the same underlying variability. Similar patterns are observed for d = 8 d=8 and larger values of n n . Overall, these results highlight the inherent sensitivity of MILP solvers to constraint tightness. Detailed results are presented in Appendix A – Figures 9 , 9 , and 7 .

Regarding RQ5 — As shown in Figure 4 , both 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} and 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} exhibit similar performance in the single-group setting. As the tuple size increases, the runtime grows approximately linearly with n n . Notably, we are able to find a realizable function explaining the ranking for all 300,000 tuples within the 1800-second timeout. While 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} scales up to 150,000 tuples, 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} remains tractable up to 275,000 tuples.

sections.heading: Results: RQ7 – Quality of Explanations
sections.text: Finally, we evaluate explanation quality across all datasets. As mentioned while discussing datasets, for the synthetic datasets, both the data and the underlying linear function are known, allowing a precise assessment of reconstruction accuracy. Similarly, for the JEE dataset, the injected additive bonuses and affected tuples are also known, enabling direct evaluation of recovery accuracy. Across all synthetic datasets as well as the JEE dataset, the solutions produced by 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝚁𝚎𝚏𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚍 \mathtt{MILP_{Refined}} and 𝙼𝙸𝙻𝙿 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \mathtt{MILP_{Base}} exactly recover the added bonuses and the corresponding tuples. These results indicate that the MILP-based formulations scale effectively to large real-world datasets while maintaining high solution quality.

sections.heading: 7. Related Work
sections.text: Utility functions : Many classes of utility functions have been explored in prior work. Monotone utility functions ( Fagin, 2002 ) form one such class: given two tuples t i t_{i} and t j t_{j} where t i ​ [ x ] > t j ​ [ x ] t_{i}[x]>t_{j}[x] for every attribute x x , the function assigns a higher score to t i t_{i} than to t j t_{j} . Efficient Top- k k evaluation for monotone functions was investigated by Fagin et al. ( Fagin et al., 2001 ) , who proposed the Threshold and Fagin’s algorithms. Along similar lines, Xin et al. ( Xin et al., 2006 ) study Top- k k computation under user preferences over selected attributes, modeled as convex functions. Beyond convexity, non-linear utility functions have also been examined, including quadratic functions ( Kessler Faulkner et al., 2015 ) and more general polynomial functions ( Qi et al., 2018 ) in multi-criteria Top- k k settings. Among the many families of utility functions, linear functions have been especially influential, forming a core component of multi-criteria decision making ( Nanongkai et al., 2010 ) , ranking and interactive scoring systems ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , and the interpretation of complex machine learning models ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ) . While non-linear, monotone, and other function classes have been used for Top- k k generation, work on utility and scoring frameworks ( Shetiya et al., 2019 ; Asudeh et al., 2019a ) has predominantly focused on linear functions. Following this well-established line of research, where linear functions serve as standard models for utility and scoring ( Shetiya et al., 2019 ; Nanongkai et al., 2010 ) , we also use linear functions as the scoring model in our work with additive bonuses. Learning ranking functions : Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2025 ) propose RankHow , which explains an observed ranking using a linear function chosen to minimize Spearman’s footrule distance from π \pi . Their formulation, however, does not allow additive bonuses, and thus may fail to realize π \pi when tuples must be organized into at most g g groups receiving group-wise boosts, as required in g g -GBLR . Fair ranking approaches ( Asudeh et al., 2019a ; Cai, 2025 ) also learn linear utility functions but focus solely on satisfying group fairness constraints in the top- k k positions, without modeling additive adjustments. Work on reverse top- k k queries ( Vlachou et al., 2010 ) is also related, seeking linear functions under which specified tuples appear in the top- k k . Why-not queries ( He and Lo, 2014 ) similarly search for a linear function that places a designated tuple within the top- k k , while other formulations ( Liu et al., 2016 ) assume a fixed set of linear functions and aim to minimally modify tuples so that they enter or exit the top- k k . These approaches, however, do not incorporate additive bonuses and thus do not generalize to our setting; moreover, they only explain top- k k behavior for selected tuples and do not address the problem of explaining a complete ranking. Traditional regression techniques – such as linear models ( Maulud and Abdulazeez, 2020 ) , decision trees ( Charbuty and Abdulazeez, 2021 ) , and neural networks ( Lee et al., 2022 ) – require numeric labels and thus cannot be applied when only an ordering is available. Additionally, extension of these techniques to make them bonus-aware is not straightforward and can be an interesting work in itself. Model-agnostic explanation tools like LIME ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ) and its related IR approaches ( Verma and Ganguly, 2019 ) , produce explanations by querying the underlying model through sampling of data points around the query point, which is infeasible in our setting where the ranking function is unknown . Our work is the first to study the problem of bonus-aware linear ranking functions as a model of explanation of a given ranking.

sections.heading: 8. Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: In this work, we look at explanations to ranking problems based on linear scoring functions with an additive bonus model. An interesting direction is to extend or design new methods for other classes of ranking functions, such as quadratic/non-linear utility functions. Another promising open direction is to consider different models for bonus, for instance, a multiplicative bonus model, where each tuple’s bonus would be computed by f w ​ ( t ) = b ​ o ​ n ​ u ​ s ​ ( t ⁡ [ τ ] ) ⋅ ( ∑ j = 1 d w j ⋅ t ⁡ [ j ] ) . f_{w}(t)=bonus(t[\tau])\cdot\left(\sum\nolimits_{j=1}^{d}w_{j}\cdot t[j]\right). While our ERMB approach and the hardness results apply also to the multiplicative model, our extension to g g -GBLR , and the ILP-based approaches do not extend. An interesting avenue of research is to design efficient algorithms for the multiplicative-bonus setting. In this paper, we show that no efficient algorithm can exactly solve the bonus-aware linear ranking explanation problem. This hardness result suggests a natural next step: can we design algorithms that achieve a small approximation (in the number of bonus groups)? Or, under standard complexity assumptions, can we prove that even such approximations are impossible? The latter appears especially relevant given our MILP formulation, which points to a close connection with the classical Max- k k -LIN problem, for which strong hardness-of-approximation results are known (e.g., ( Arora et al., 1997 ; Khot et al., 2007 ; O’Donnell et al., 2011 ; Bhangale and Khot, 2021 ) ). This, in turn, raises the question of whether approximation algorithms for the bonus-aware linear ranking explanation problem are likewise unattainable.

In our running example, a user would be interested in obtaining the best quality computer at the least price. To uniformly deal with such cases, we normalize the attribute score of “ price " (in general, any negatively contributing attribute A A ), of each item t t by t ⁡ [ A ] = max j ⁡ ( t j ​ [ A ] ) − t ⁡ [ A ] max j ⁡ ( t j ​ [ A ] ) − min j ⁡ ( t j ​ [ A ] ) t[A]=\frac{\max_{j}(t_{j}[A])-t[A]}{\max_{j}(t_{j}[A])-\min_{j}(t_{j}[A])} Once normalized, the weight of each attribute in the utility function can be restricted to positive values. sections.text: Lemma 1. ERMB (Algorithm 1 ) has a time complexity of 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ d + 1 ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2d+1}\log n) . Proof. Algorithm 1 introduces a hyperplane for every pair of tuples t i t_{i} , t j t_{j} . As stated before, this forms a central arrangement and partitions the d d -dimensional space into n 2 ​ ( d − 1 ) n^{2(d-1)} disjoint regions. In our ( d − 1 ) (d-1) dimensional space, enumeration of each of the cells can be performed using the enumeration algorithm in Rada et al. ( Rada and Cerny, 2018 ) . ( Rada and Cerny, 2018 ) computes a Linear Program with d d variables and n 2 n^{2} constraints in every cell. Meggido ( Megiddo, 1984 ) proposes a linear-time algorithm for solving an LP in fixed dimension d d . Combining the two results, the enumeration process consumes a total of 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2d}) time. In every region, using the weight vector returned by the LP, the scores for the n n tuples are computed in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(nd) time. Based on the scores, sorting is performed to obtain a ranking ρ \rho . Thus, in every region, 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n\log{n}) time is consumed to construct the ranking ρ \rho . Upon computing the ranking ρ \rho , LIS is computed on ρ \rho in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n\log{n}) time. Thus, the overall time spent in a single region is 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n\log{n}) time. As there are n 2 ​ d − 2 n^{2d-2} regions, our algorithm consumes a total of 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ d + 1 ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2d+1}\log n) time. ∎

sections.text: We now present arguments for correctness and time complexity bounds for our algorithm. Theorem 1. The running time of MGRA (Algorithm 2 ) is 𝒪 ⁡ ( g 2 ​ ( d + g ) ⋅ n 2 ​ ( d + g ) ) \mathcal{O}\left(g^{2(d+g)}\cdot n^{2(d+g)}\right) . Proof. Observe that for each point in 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , we create g g additional points in 𝒟 G \mathcal{D}_{G} . So | 𝒟 G | = n ⁡ ( g + 1 ) |\mathcal{D}_{G}|=n(g+1) . As the dimension of the weight-space has changed to d + g d+g with ( n ⁡ ( g + 1 ) ) 2 (n(g+1))^{2} hyperplanes, the number of possible regions of the central arrangement is 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( n ⁡ ( g + 1 ) ) 2 ​ ( d − 1 + g ) ) \mathcal{O}((n(g+1))^{2(d-1+g)}) . Similar to Theorem 1 , the regions are enumerated using ( Rada and Cerny, 2018 ) , with the LP consuming 𝒪 ⁡ ( n 2 ​ g 2 ) \mathcal{O}(n^{2}g^{2}) time per region, and then solving the LCS problem on the realized ranking ρ \rho . Now consider the running time of the DP to compute the LCS. It holds that k ≤ n k\leq n . Therefore, the number of states in the DP is upper bounded by 𝒪 ⁡ ( g ​ n 2 ) \mathcal{O}(gn^{2}) , and each state is solvable in 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) time. Therefore, the overall runtime of the algorithm is upper bounded by 𝒪 ⁡ ( g 2 ​ ( d + g ) ⋅ n 2 ​ ( d + g ) ) \mathcal{O}(g^{2(d+g)}\cdot n^{2(d+g)}) . ∎ Theorem 2. Given P , π , k P,\pi,k , if there exists a satisfying solution to g g -GBLR , then MGRA (Algorithm 2 ) returns a vector w ∈ ℝ d w\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , v 1 , … , v g ∈ ℝ + v_{1},...,v_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} and disjoint G 1 , … , G g ⊂ P G_{1},...,G_{g}\subset P with ∑ i ∈ G ≤ k \sum_{i\in G}\leq k which satisfies the problem. Proof. Suppose that there does exist some vector w ∗ w^{*} , groups G 1 ∗ , … , G g ∗ ⊂ P G^{*}_{1},...,G^{*}_{g}\subset P , and additive values v 1 ∗ , … , v g ∗ v^{*}_{1},...,v^{*}_{g} that satisfy the given input. Consider the region in the arrangement of ℋ \mathcal{H} where w ∗ w^{*} is located. Let v ∗ v^{*} be the optimal bonus scores. Consider the ranking σ \sigma over 𝒟 G \mathcal{D}_{G} caused by this partition. As w ∗ w^{*} and v ∗ v^{*} must lie in one of the regions of the arrangement, an LCS of ρ \rho and π \pi must definitely be explored. The constrained LCS problem between ρ \rho and π \pi can be solved exactly. Based on this, we can obtain both the ranking function w ∗ w^{*} and the bonus scores v ∗ v^{*} along with the group information. Hence, our algorithm finds a satisfying solution if one exists. ∎

Determining a linear utility function that correlates with observed candidate rankings is a foundational problem with applications in domains such as admissions, hiring, and recommendation systems, e.g., [Storandt and Funke, AAAI’19, Zhang et al., KDD’23, Wang et al., ICDE’24 (best paper award), Chen and Wong, VLDB’24]. Traditionally, these models assume full visibility into the feature sets used to determine the utility score. However, real-world scenarios often involve sensitive attributes that are hidden or partially observed, yet may influence outcomes through additive bonuses designed to promote fairness, as in [Gale and Marian, ICDE’24]. Motivated by such practical concerns, we study a variant of the ranking explanation problem where sensitive features are unobserved but may influence candidate rankings through group-specific linear boosts. We present a formal framework for modeling this problem and develop an algorithmic solution that leverages constraint satisfaction and automated reasoning techniques to jointly infer the linear scoring parameters and latent group bonuses consistent with the observed rankings. We further show that determining a satisfying linear function with group-specific bonuses is NP -hard in general, but when the feature dimension and the number of groups are constant, the problem admits a polynomial-time solution. Our approach is the first to address this nuanced variant, which captures key real-world challenges in fair ranking and admission systems. We perform extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets, demonstrating that our method effectively recovers hidden bonus structures and provides faithful explanations of observed ranking outcomes. Keywords: Explainable Ranking, Linear Utility Models, Hidden Group Bonuses, Hyperplane Arrangements, Mixed Integer Linear Programming † † cc-license: by Resource Availability: The source code of this paper has been made publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20322450 . 1. Introduction Ranking algorithms are central to numerous AI applications, including web search, recommender systems, and information retrieval. However, despite their pervasive use, the decision-making processes behind these algorithms often remain opaque, which raises critical concerns around trust, fairness, and accountability. As a result, explainability in ranking has emerged as a pressing research challenge within the AI community. Several recent works have sought to adapt principles from interpretable machine learning to the ranking setting ( Chowdhury et al., 2023 ; Chowdhury et al., 2025 ; Heuss et al., 2025 ) , aiming to generate faithful, user-understandable explanations for ranked outputs. Some approaches focus on post-hoc explanations, while others design models that are easier to interpret from the start ( Singh and Joachims, 2019 ; Ai et al., 2018 ) . There is also increasing attention to broader goals like fairness and trust in ranked results ( Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017 ; Rampisela et al., 2024 ) . Yet, many basic questions remain open: what does it mean for a ranking to be explainable? How do we measure the quality of an explanation when the output is an ordered list instead of a single label? Modeling user preferences is a central challenge in multi-criteria decision-making. A common and effective approach is to formalize these preferences with a utility function that assigns a numerical score/utility to each candidate, thereby inducing a natural ordering. Candidates are typically characterized by a set of features, which can be distinguished as scoring attributes – that directly contribute to utility, and sensitive attributes – used to enforce auxiliary goals such as fairness or diversity. Among various functional forms, linear utility models are arguably the most widely adopted. Their prevalence stems from a powerful combination of simplicity and practical efficacy. The straightforward structure of a weighted sum not only facilitates deployment in large-scale systems like web search and recommender engines ( Morik et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2023 ; Thonet et al., 2022 ) but also offers inherent transparency ( Sen et al., 2020 ; Gale and Marian, 2020 ) . This transparency, simplicity, and effectiveness make linear utility-based models a natural starting point for research into explainability and learning to rank ( Asudeh et al., 2019b ; Chen and Wong, 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , interactive learning ( Nanongkai et al., 2012 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , reverse regret ( Wang et al., 2024 ) (best paper award at ICDE’24), and the integration of fairness and diversity mechanisms ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Despite their simplicity, linear utilities have demonstrated competitive performance, confirming their status as a robust and versatile modeling choice, e.g., ( Qian et al., 2015 ; Storandt and Funke, 2019 ) . We refer the readers to Section 7 for a more elaborate discussion on related works. Several works have studied how to quantify the distance between a given ranking and one induced by a (linear) utility function. Common notions include the number of violated pairwise orders, the distance to a consistent utility vector, and the minimum perturbation needed to make the ranking “linearizable”. Exact computation is often intractable in the presence of conflicting preferences, motivating the study of approximation and structural relaxations (e.g., ( Dwork et al., 2001 ; Davenport and Kalagnanam, 2004 ) ). In many real-life scenarios, a small additive bonus is essential to ensure that a linear utility-based ranking model aligns with observed outcomes. Such a bonus is primarily calculated based on the sensitive attributes ( Shetiya et al., 2022 ; Asudeh et al., 2019a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) – separate from the scoring attributes used to compute utility – associated with each candidate or item. This often arises when external goals, such as affirmative action, fairness constraints, or prior trust scores, must be incorporated uniformly across items of certain groups. The application of compensatory additive bonuses to linear utilities is an approach that has been explored for promoting fairness in ranking systems ( Gale and Marian, 2024 ) . Without such a term, even simple adjustments to promote underrepresented groups may not be achievable within the linear feature space, making the additive bonus a minimal yet powerful mechanism for enforcing policy-driven interventions (see ( Mathioudakis et al., 2020 ) ). We motivate our problem with the following running example of diversity in University admissions. Example dataset of eight university applicants. Example 1 (University admissions). Consider a public university conducting its annual admissions, where applicants are ranked using a linear utility-based model . Academic performance is assessed through multiple indicators, such as entrance test and SAT scores, which are normalized, weighted, and linearly aggregated to compute a base utility score. As a public institution committed to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), the university augments this model with an additive incentive mechanism . Recognizing that applicants from underprivileged (UP) backgrounds may face structural disadvantages affecting academic performance, an expert committee assigns a group-specific bonus score. This bonus is added to the base utility score of each applicant in the corresponding group, yielding an adjusted utility score that determines the final ranking. For example, suppose eight applicants apply, as shown in Table 1 . The candidates are ranked c 2 c_{2} , c 3 c_{3} , c 1 c_{1} , c 5 c_{5} , c 6 c_{6} , c 7 c_{7} , c 4 , c 8 c_{4},c_{8} based on their adjusted utility scores. Given only anonymized public data (academic indicators and rankings), third-party auditors aim to explain the observed outcomes under this linear utility function with additive group-level bonuses . The sensitive attributes, such as group membership (Column 2 of Table 1 ), and the exact bonus values are not disclosed. Problem (Informal) Formulation Given a ranking, can it be explained by a linear utility function with a small number of additive bonuses? In the Singleton Group Bonus Linear Ranking ( SGBLR ) version, arbitrary bonuses may be given to at most k k items. In the g g -Group Bonus Linear Ranking ( g g -GBLR ) version, there are g g (special) groups each containing a limited number of items, and group-specific bonuses – each item of a particular group gets the same amount as a bonus, and bonus value for different groups could be different – are allowed. The goal is to find weights and bonus assignments that reproduce the ranking exactly. Note that Example 1 is for the 1 1 -GBLR variant with one (special) group being UP – all the candidates of the UP group receive an additive bonus of the same amount. Our method conceptually builds upon seminal works LIME ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ) and SHAP ( Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ) , which infer feature contributions to predictions, as our model learns weights for each feature, which provides an explanation for the observed ranking. It extends this line of work by modeling hidden additive bonuses beyond observable features as part of the explanation. We envision our technique as contributing to the broader area of trustworthy and responsible data science, particularly in applications such as algorithmic auditing and explainability. For example, in an auditing setting, suppose a ranking model is used to evaluate candidates, and there is a requirement that all candidates within the same group receive identical bonuses. If our method is unable to recover a linear utility function with such additive bonuses that explains the observed ranking, this serves as evidence that the ranking violates the intended fairness constraint. Alternatively, our framework can be used for interpretability. If an observed ranking can be well-approximated by our model, the learned weights provide insight into the relative importance of different attributes, while the inferred additive bonuses reveal how much advantage may have been assigned to specific candidates. This can help assess whether such adjustments are reasonable within the given domain and context. 1.1. Our Contributions In this paper, we initiate a formal study on the problem of learning a linear utility function with small additive group-wise bonuses that realizes a given ranking. On the theoretical side, we provide exact algorithms and establish computational hardness. Next, we address the question of designing scalable algorithms that work efficiently in practice. More specifically, we show the following results. • We start by considering the singleton group variant ( SGBLR ) that captures the allowance of arbitrary (potentially different) additive bonuses to a few individual items. We design a hyperplane-based algorithm – enumerating over all the regions specified by a set of comparison hyperplanes, and then performing certain longest common subsequence (LCS) computation in each region. Our algorithm works in polynomial time for constant-dimensional points. However, such geometric reasoning scales poorly with the number of data points n n and dimensions d d , since the number of combinatorial regions grows exponentially.
